case_law.Court / citation: 535 F.3d 1373 (Fed. Cir. 2008) (No. 2008-1001), on appeal from N.D. Cal. No. 06-cv-1905
case_law.Holding / status: Artistic License terms are enforceable copyright conditions (not mere covenants), so use outside them can be copyright infringement. Preliminary-injunction appeal; vacated and remanded
case_law.Why it matters: Foundation for OSS license enforceability in U.S.

case_law.Court / citation: N.D. Cal. No. 5:18-cv-07182-EJD; 9th Cir. No. 21-16029 (unpublished memo); 9th Cir. No. 24-5538
case_law.Date(s): May 18, 2021 (N.D. Cal. partial summary judgment on §7/§10); Feb. 18, 2022 (9th Cir. memo affirming preliminary injunction); July 22, 2024 (findings: US$597,000 actual damages, permanent injunction); Aug. 15, 2024 (judgment: plus $57,288 prejudgment interest, less stipulated $26,000); Dec. 10, 2025 (9th Cir. No. 24-5538 dismissed on stipulated voluntary dismissal); Dec. 15, 2025 (satisfaction of judgment)
case_law.Holding / status: District court: a licensor may combine AGPLv3 with the Commons Clause; AGPL §7/§10 bar further restrictions only by licensees ("you"), so licensees cannot strip licensor-imposed terms. Liability ran on Lanham Act and DMCA §1202(b) claims. Non-precedential: the 9th Cir. memo endorsed the §7 reading only in affirming a preliminary injunction; no appellate merits ruling on §7
case_law.Why it matters: Do not assume "AGPL + rider" can be cleaned to plain AGPL

case_law.Case: Software Freedom Conservancy v. Vizio, Inc.
case_law.Court / citation: Cal. Super. Ct., Orange County, No. 30-2021-01226723-CU-BC-CJC
case_law.Date(s): Mar. 26, 2024 (third-party-beneficiary status held a triable issue); Dec. 23, 2025 (minute order granting Vizio's summary adjudication); trial set for Jan. 12, 2026 was vacated Jan. 8, 2026, then reset for Aug. 10-19, 2026; on Aug. 9, 2026 SFC moved its listed trial date to "late 2026" (party statement; court docket not checked)
case_law.Holding / status: Pretrial summary-adjudication order: GPLv2/LGPLv2.1 require source to be provided so it can be obtained and modified (source is defined to include installation scripts), but impose no duty to enable reinstallation of modified software such that the TVs continue to function properly. Whether purchasers can enforce as third-party beneficiaries remains a triable issue. Trial court ruling, not precedential. As of Nov. 23, 2026 SFC lists the case as ongoing with trial expected in late 2026; no verdict, judgment or settlement has been reported (per SFC, a party; docket not checked)
case_law.Why it matters: Consumer (third-party beneficiary) enforcement; GPLv2 vs GPLv3 installation duties
case_law.Verification status: Verified (primary) for 2024 and Dec. 2025 orders; trial status secondary only

case_law.Case: Artifex Software, Inc. v. Hancom, Inc.
case_law.Date(s): Apr. 25, 2017 (motion to dismiss denied); Sept. 12, 2017 (partial summary judgment on contract remedies denied); Jan. 17, 2018 (stipulated dismissal with prejudice after confidential settlement)
case_law.Holding / status: At the pleading stage, the court held that Artifex adequately alleged the GPL formed an enforceable contract and that the contract claim was not preempted by copyright, alongside a copyright claim (dual-licensed Ghostscript). It later refused to rule out contract damages as a matter of law. No merits ruling; settled
case_law.Why it matters: Contract damages theory for GPL non-compliance
case_law.Verification status: Verified (primary) for the 2017 orders; dismissal date from docket mirror (PacerMonitor)

case_law.Court / citation: Cour d'appel de Paris, pôle 5, ch. 1, RG n° 22/18071 (on remand after Cass. 1re civ., Oct. 5, 2022, n° 21-15.386)
case_law.Holding / status: Orange and Orange Business Services held liable for copyright infringement (contrefaçon) of the LASSO library by violating GPLv2 (arts. 2, 3, 4, 10) and the author's attribution right; ordered to pay EUR 800,000 in damages (500,000 economic loss, 150,000 moral harm, 150,000 infringer profits) plus EUR 60,000 in procedural costs
case_law.Why it matters: EU enforcement; large damages for GPL non-compliance
case_law.Verification status: Secondary only (two matching full-text copies of the judgment: Interoperable Europe, Legalis; the court's own copy was not reached)

case_law.Court / citation: 9th Cir. No. 24-7700 (published opinion; § 1292(b) interlocutory appeal); N.D. Cal. No. 4:22-cv-06823-JST
case_law.Holding / status: Affirmed dismissal of DMCA §1202(b) claim: on plaintiffs' own allegations, Copilot/Codex create new works rather than removing or altering CMI from copies of existing works. "Identicality" is a misnomer - an evidentiary gloss, not an element; substantial (even non-identical) reproduction without CMI can support an inference of removal. Plaintiffs had standing. "Input" (training-data) theory forfeited, not decided. Contract claims remain pending in district court
case_law.Why it matters: Narrows DMCA attribution claims against AI coding tools; retrieval-style systems may be treated differently; the court expressed no view on copyright infringement, and license (contract) claims continue

case_law.Court / citation: Travis County, Tex. (53rd Judicial District Court); W.D. Tex. Nos. 1:14-cv-00012-SS and 1:14-cv-00221-SS
case_law.Date(s): Nov. 13, 2012 (filed); Mar. 11, 2014 (W.D. Tex. preemption ruling and remand); Apr. 25, 2014 (dismissed with prejudice on joint motion)
case_law.Holding / status: Customer's counterclaim that the vendor breached GPLv2 (embedded XimpleWare VTD-XML) held not preempted by the Copyright Act, because the source-disclosure promise is an extra element. Third-party-beneficiary standing not decided. Case dismissed with prejudice on joint motion; no merits ruling on the GPL
case_law.Why it matters: GPL as a counterclaim risk in commercial software disputes; GPL obligations can be litigated as state-law contract claims

case_law.Case: HashiCorp, Inc. / OpenTofu (cease-and-desist and DMCA notice over the "removed" block)
case_law.Court / citation: No court filing; cease-and-desist letter from HashiCorp's counsel, GitHub DMCA takedown notice, and OpenTofu DMCA counter notice
case_law.Date(s): Apr. 3, 2024 (cease-and-desist; response demanded by Apr. 10); Apr. 9, 2024 (OpenTofu counsel's response); Apr. 11, 2024 (OpenTofu publishes the letters and a source code origin analysis; date of HashiCorp's DMCA notice in GitHub's DMCA repository); Apr. 24, 2024 (OpenTofu DMCA counter notice)
case_law.Holding / status: No ruling. HashiCorp asserted that five OpenTofu files implementing the "removed" block copied BUSL-1.1 Terraform code and were relabeled MPL-2.0, named the contributors involved, demanded removal, and reserved DMCA takedowns and litigation. OpenTofu's counsel and published analysis stated the files derive from pre-fork MPL-2.0 code; OpenTofu filed a DMCA counter notice. No later demand by HashiCorp or IBM (owner since Feb. 27, 2025) appears in either party's records, and the disputed file remains in the OpenTofu repository as of Nov. 23, 2026. No lawsuit announced by either party (docket not checked)
case_law.Why it matters: Forks of relicensed projects: document the origin of code against the last permissively licensed version, and expect copyright and SPDX header choices in new files to be scrutinized
case_law.Verification status: Partially verified (primary): parties' own records; court docket not checked

case_law.Case: Ascensio System SIA (ONLYOFFICE) / Nextcloud, IONOS and the Euro-Office project (AGPLv3 Section 7 logo-retention term)
case_law.Court / citation: No court filing; public license dispute conducted through the parties' blog posts, an ONLYOFFICE partnership suspension, and license and header changes on GitHub
case_law.Date(s): Mar. 27, 2026 (Euro-Office launched; logo-retention term removed from its headers); Mar. 30, 2026 (ONLYOFFICE asserts license violation and copyright infringement); Mar. 31, 2026 (ONLYOFFICE suspends Nextcloud partnership); Apr. 15, 2026 (FSF statement); Apr. 17, 2026 (Nextcloud compliance analysis); Apr. 21, 2026 (ONLYOFFICE open letter); May 6, 2026 (ONLYOFFICE replaces its LICENSE additional terms); Aug. 18, 2026 (Nextcloud says it will conform to the new license)
case_law.Holding / status: No ruling. ONLYOFFICE asserted that its Section 7(b) term requiring retention of the product logo is part of an indivisible grant, so removing it breaches AGPLv3 and terminates rights under Section 8. Nextcloud asserted the term is a "further restriction" that Section 7 lets recipients remove, and the FSF publicly took the same view. On May 6, 2026 ONLYOFFICE replaced the logo term with attribution, modification-notice and user-interface notice terms plus a trademark disclaimer; on Aug. 18, 2026 Nextcloud stated it would update Euro-Office code and headers to match. No lawsuit announced by either party (docket not checked)
case_law.Why it matters: AGPLv3 additional terms: the FSF's published view is that a logo-retention requirement is not a permitted Section 7(b) term and may be removed as a further restriction; licensors seeking attribution are pointed to author-attribution notices and Section 7(e) trademark terms instead
case_law.Verification status: Partially verified (primary): parties' own records; court docket not checked

regulatory.Key dates: GPAI obligations (Chapter V, incl. Arts. 53-54) apply from Aug. 2, 2025 (Art. 113, third para., point (b)); GPAI models placed on the market before Aug. 2, 2025 must comply by Aug. 2, 2027 (Art. 111(3)); Commission fining powers over GPAI providers (Art. 101) apply from Aug. 2, 2026 (Art. 113, second para.). These dates are unchanged by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Reg. (EU) 2026/1744).
regulatory.OSS-relevant rule: Art. 53(2) exempts only technical documentation (53(1)(a)) and information for downstream providers (53(1)(b)); Art. 54(6) exempts the authorised-representative duty for non-EU providers. Conditions: release under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution of the model, with parameters (including weights), model-architecture information and model-usage information made publicly available. Under recital 103, components provided against a price or otherwise monetised do not benefit. Copyright policy (53(1)(c)), training-content summary (53(1)(d)) and cooperation with the Commission and authorities (53(3)) still apply. Neither exemption applies to GPAI models with systemic risk, which also carry Art. 55 duties.
regulatory.Diligence / compliance action: Do not assume an "open-weight" model qualifies: the Commission guidelines (C(2025) 7719, adopted Nov. 19, 2025; content approved July 18, 2025) treat non-commercial or research-only limits, distribution bans, user-scale thresholds and separate commercial licences for specific uses as disqualifying, and dual licensing or mandatory paid access as monetisation. The guidelines are not binding.

regulatory.Key dates: In force Dec. 10, 2024 (Art. 71(1); OJ 20.11.2024); Art. 14 reporting applies from Sept. 11, 2026 (Art. 71(2)), including to products placed on the market before Dec. 11, 2027 (Art. 69(3)); Chapter IV (conformity assessment bodies) from June 11, 2026; full application Dec. 11, 2027 (Art. 71(2)). Steward obligations (Art. 24, including reporting under Art. 24(3)) have no separate date; on our reading of Art. 71(2) they apply from Dec. 11, 2027 (no article states this directly).
regulatory.OSS-relevant rule: Manufacturers must notify actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents simultaneously to the coordinating CSIRT and ENISA via the single reporting platform (Art. 14): early warning within 24h; notification within 72h; final report within 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available (vulnerabilities) or within one month after the incident notification (severe incidents). Manufacturers must also inform impacted users (Art. 14(8)). Micro and small enterprises are not fined for missing the 24h deadline (Art. 64(10)(a)). Art. 3(14) defines the "open-source software steward": a legal person, other than a manufacturer, that provides sustained support for free and open-source software intended for commercial activities. Under Art. 24 a steward must keep a documented cybersecurity policy, cooperate with market surveillance authorities, report under Art. 14(1) to the extent involved in development, and report under Art. 14(3) and (8) for severe incidents affecting its own development infrastructure. Stewards face no administrative fines (Art. 64(10)(b)).
regulatory.Diligence / compliance action: Confirm, product by product, whether the target is a manufacturer or an open-source software steward; vulnerability handling process; SBOM covering at least top-level dependencies (Annex I, Part II(1)); 24h/72h reporting readiness from Sept. 11, 2026, including for products already on the market

regulatory.Instrument: OMB M-26-05 (Adopting a Risk-based Approach to Software and Hardware Security)
regulatory.OSS-relevant rule: Rescinds M-22-18 and M-23-16, so the Secure Software Development Attestation Form (Common Form) is no longer required government-wide, though agencies may still choose to use it; agencies must keep complete software and hardware inventories and set risk-based assurance policies, and may adopt contract terms requiring a current SBOM on request (for cloud platforms, of the runtime production environment)
regulatory.Diligence / compliance action: Check each solicitation/contract for attestation or SBOM clauses
